title: A Personal Experience with Coralie Fargeat's The Substance.

commenti.body: [removed]

I thought the practical effects were good but I didn’t think it had anything new to say in any meaningful or thought provoking way. It was one note that beat you over the head for 45 minutes too long.

In psychology there’s an interesting distinction made between the ideal ego — how we imagine we appear to others — and the ego ideal — the image of who we desire to be. 

These two images are often in conflict, and The Substance makes the conflict very literal — the more unrealistic Elisabeth’s pursuit of an idealized image becomes, the more her actual self image suffers, the more fractured and disassociated her identity becomes.

And what’s really interesting with aging, or with balding, is at some point the ego ideal can become a former ideal ego, a past self image is projected into a future desire to the extent that looking in the mirror makes you feel haunted.

Hair loss treatment ads (or weight loss or anti aging) always seem to prey on this logic — they always show us an image of a divided self — an  image of an unhappy bald man beside an image of the same man smiling, fully coiffured. To the balding man, the second image is in the past, but of course the ad will reverse this, labeling the second image “after.”

I thought the substance played out this psychic conflict between dual self images with amazing lucidity, which makes it easy for everyone to relate to, we all have trouble reconciling how we imagine we appear to others with how we want to appear. Great write up, showing how we can apply the logic of the movie in a more universal way.
I think the bludgeoning was the point. I agree I definitely felt the length but the way it keeps doubling down is admirable.

As a mid-fifties male with grey hair watching this I became acutely aware that I was one of the stare holders, men of more senior years invested in their gratification by way of fresh meat from the entertainment mill. Of all the many close ups, those of Dennis Quaid masticating were the most telling. Unapologetically chewing up all that was in front of him, without a moment of thought as to the consequences. I thought the leads were superb in their roles. Both wanted more, each however had to pay for their hunger. There's nothing wrong with bludgeoning an audience with a message, it makes certain that it's received.

> I agree I definitely felt the length

I stopped when I'd seen enough, which turned out was exactly at the 50% mark. I appreciated that it went full retard (in a good way) and pulled no punches. I agree and disagree with /u/Nongenerate about it having anything new to say. I don't think the film had anything at all new to say, but that's not what films always have to be. Most films don't have anything new to say, there aren't usually new things to say. 

The film (or at least the first half) said a very well-known, well-worn thing, in a fun way. I'd never seen this retread of an idea told in this delightfully unapologetic manner. It was relentless and never got cold feet. It was just too long for me, you don't always have to join the clean plate club.
Thank you for the wonderful information.

Substance is a modern, well-done B-movie. Could've been greatly elevated with some interesting themes besides 'Hollywood objectifies' and I'm surprised people are hailing those aspects as visionary. 

Felt like Fargeat was kinda trying the upfront absurdism thing a la The Lobster/Lanthimos, and it worked somewhat. I still would've loved walking away with deeper questions and understandings.

I think besides all the body horror, the most enduring scene in the movie is Elizabeth getting ready for her date and how heartbreaking and upsetting and relatable it is. It’s the point of no return for her. I think that scene especially is meaningful and thought provoking, at least to a “general” audience. “Barbie” isn’t a perfect comparison but the way it weaved some digestible feminist ideology into a blockbuster about a toy is commendable

I agree that “duality” is integral to the formation of our self-image. We compare our bodies at 30 with our bodies at 20, just like we may compare our level of ‘desirability’ to the beacons of ‘hotness’ reinforced by celebrity culture and mainstream beauty standards.

And while the movie dives deep into the physical and psychological horrors the human body is subjected to delay the aging process and achieve the desired external ‘qualities’ in favor of outside validation, there’s also an underlying message in favor of self-care.

Before discovering the Substance, we can assume Elisabeth had access to all sorts of cosmetic procedures, skin-care routines, and vitamin and diet plans. When she begins aging rapidly, her ‘old’, degraded version is the consequence of spending something like 4 decades without tending to her body’s needs and without any aid of modern medicine and cosmetology.

I really enjoyed the first 2/3rds of the movie, but the finale fell flat for me.  After Sue attempts to reuse the Substance and we get the Cronenberg Monstro version, it felt sort of like they didn't know how to end the movie.  I personally would have probably ended it with Sue just dying on stage during the New Years Eve show, with maybe everyone just continuing as if this was all part of the show.  I guess that feels a bit cliche, but that's why I'm not a writer/director.  

The literally minutes long fountain of blood felt... I dunno, it rolled over past squick into "okay, I can't even take this remotely seriously now." for me.

This movie was tremendous in terms of visual style, practical effects and acting.

I felt the weakest part of the film was the writing. Demi Moore did a phenomenal job however her character lacked depth, relationships, or a meaningful arc.

There were many contrived moments. Moments engineered to show us more body horror even though they went against character development. Stylistic shots that betrayed the story. 

Overall a very enjoyable experience with a powerful message that felt a little one note and a bit too long.

The undeveloped characters IMO were a narrative choice to make it seem more like a macabre fairytale. We don't know anything about the characters in a fairy tale - as it's only really a device to deliver a warning or a lesson.

First off, Demi Moore will always be so irrevocably A-list that she can literally act in any old thing, basically, and people will still give her her iconic props.

For me, the worst part was expecting a >!shiny new self to emerge even up to the very end.!< That's on me, I guess. Yet if others feel >!the ketchup on the star was a respectful, thoughtful foreshadowing of the gore that was to wind up on it later!< and called that tying everything together nicely, then what can I say.

Personally,  I guess I felt like the investment would pay off in a >!realistically horrific ending!< and not the >!gore-filled fever dream.!< we wound up with.  

Like cinematic collagen plumping things up grotesquely -- it kind of sacrificed the pure, stark & macabre beauty with which it had begun.

The script is flawed. Sue knows she’s killing Elisabeth, and that if Elisabeth dies, she dies. Yet she doesn’t reel it back in. A fatal craving for stardom doesn’t cut it, I just can’t suspend that disbelief. It’s either a desperate obsession for Sue to thoughtlessly seek mega stardom at her own expense, or the writer and director are trying to tell us Sue is stupid and doesn’t know how death works. Both are equally dumb. And I’m sorry for my coarse words, but Acts II and III are insulting to the audience. You can’t reconcile Sue’s motivation for super stardom, with suicidality, and stupidity is equally as inane. And although I respect Moore’s fondness of Qualley, you can’t compare their skill levels.

> Could've been greatly elevated with some interesting themes besides 'Hollywood objectifies' and I'm surprised people are hailing those aspects as visionary.

Well, the reason it's being hailed is because there is in fact a lot more going on with it than just "Hollywood objectifies." Hollywood is only the source of like 30% of Elizabeth/Sue's problems; the real source of fun for me is the way it plays on the Evil Witch/Snow White dynamic, a tale as old as time except we rarely see it play out within a single person. The ambiguous questions of "what is the "self" here? Is it really fair to say that Sue and Elizabeth are the same person?" is compelling to me, and it's something that would still be there even if you'd taken the Hollywood aspect out of it completely. 

Even Dennis Quaid's character, who's meant to be the epitome of Hollywood greed and inhumanity, is never really the catalyst for any of Sue's choices. He happily gives her enough free time to make the seven days on/off schedule work, but Sue/Elizabeth blow it through their own greed, selfishness, self-hatred. Hollywood objectifies, sure, but it never forces Sue/Elizabeth's hand at any point. 

Not to mention that OP is a regular man not in the movie business, and he still connected with it strongly, which is a good indicator that the movie's dealing with issues far beyond just a shallow critique of Hollywood.

> Demi Moore will always be so irrevocably A-list that she can literally act in any old thing, basically, and people will still give her her iconic props.  

This doesn’t seem quite right. She was dragged for Striptease, wasn’t she? Furthermore, A-list doesn’t mean you’re immune from critique; it often means you’re more of a target when you stumble.
I agree that the underdeveloped characters were a solid narrative choice; to me they seemed to echo the hollowness of the industry itself.

Thank you for bringing this up. I feel that this is an actor's movie and they will get the metaphor of how the industry causes you to make choices at the onset and later in one's career where there is this tradeoff between young inexperienced you who would do anything for fame, even self-destructive things, and an older you desperately trying to keep the freshness of the ingenue you alive.

Just an opinion but I feel strongly about it

I'm agreeing with you how it felt weak but I think maybe the director showed us the character's inner decline through how the plot evolved and how it all felt like it was visually & emotionally falling apart. 

How else to explain to normal ppl how it feels when your beauty, your commodity, your livelihood, is fading. Like worlds colliding, like shocking decomposition. Fleeing to wild "solutions" carrying their own unique problems and symptoms, new psychoses springing from the old.
Yes! Hereditary is another movie I had to see that I was also apprehensive about and haunted by

I agree that Demi did a phenomenal job. I also agree about her character lacking depth & relationships except I feel it was to show us on a relatively uncluttered canvas the decline of this masterpiece.

I also feel that we are meant to empathise with her loneliness, her emptiness, and her commoditization: she is just a box; she is just a number; she is just a billboard; she is just a body--the objectification is obvious.

I agree about the stylism as well. Yet how heartbreaking to see her bare spine in the doctor's office, "unscathed" outwardly by the wreckage (symbolising what her career had become) yet inwardly broken (emotionally).

The poise of a dancer is everything and the spine was used as a motif both for the health of her career as well as the pursuit and  decline of her beauty.

After all, she's a throwback to the age of "Sit up straight, now", so why not use the spine itself a symbol of her bravery & her brokenness, as well as a channel for her sustenance, and her rebirth?
But why? It's clear that Sue is solely focused on getting as much fame, glory and attention as possible, Liz and her condition be damned. You can absolutely reconcile the two. It's her fatal flaw.

I am a trans woman that has to do a shot every week and I HAAATE needles. This movie was soo hard to get through. It was like dysphoria simulator.

Also I’ll be real in a way trans women probably won’t most of the time. I get terrified often that I’m like giving up this acceptable, practical, “normal” body for some unattainable ideal in my head. I’m worried it’s going to go nowhere and you know “what’s been taken can’t be given back”. Sometimes I get really dysphoric and scared of my future and look in the mirror just seeing a guy with breasts and yeah I feel like monstro. So I keep going cause I don’t want to think about it and maybe it will work out eventually. But then more will be taken. It’s really scary but like I started this for a reason. I am happy about the changes and I’m glad for whatever I can get. It’s mostly fear of others judgment because yeah when I go out I also cover myself up in a big hoodie so no one can see. 

This movie just felt extremely relatable but in the worst way possible. I had to take a shower after and I did NOT want to look in the mirror. If anything it maybe made me feel like less of a complete monster. It’s crazy cause it’s like all the trans stuff on top of the more direct patriarchal expectations stuff feels like so un-winnable. I am fairly agoraphobic and I’ve been getting really into cooking (maybe partially to feel like I can atleast fill some feminine role for my boyfriend) so her getting a cookbook like “this is all you’re good for” and her hiding away afraid of mirrors is so accurate it hurts. Also when I first met up with my boyfriend I was messing with my makeup until the very last minute and never felt pretty enough. And seeing her be confident with her younger hot body and how men treat her so different. It’s brutal. 

Worst movie ever 10/10

Great points. 

Some of my own feelings on it may have been eroded by the external expectations around it. Like watching it it felt like Elizabeth/Sue was the source of 95% of her own problems, and is a huge dirtbag on par with Dennis Quaid's character- how're you so unstable and antisocial at 50+ years old? How do you feel nothing bending the laws of nature?? But the surface level read of "it's Hollywood's fault" seemed like the *correct* answer the movie and definitely the reception wanted you to land on. 

I'd love an expansion of the non-surface themes if anybody's got them, but they still felt like afterthoughts, sprinkled in where I personally would've appreciated more focus. Haha but then again, I may just be too dumb for them. And ofc maybe it merits a second watch. 

The "is Sue/Elizabeth the same person" question is great. Many little thoughts to unpack there. 

I was also fascinated by the workout video thing. Why was that chosen to be big in this world?

I was also fascinated by the dance scenes. They seemed like they were trying to be sexy, but came off sterile and bland. Wasn't sure if that was deliberate or just a reflection on myself. 

Anyhow good comment, thanks. Fun topic of broader reaction vs intent.

I think it’s not so much what the movie said, but *how* it said it which makes it stand out. The director chose to stray from using too much nuance in her messaging, rather make everything bold and in your face - from the soundscapes, typefont, big sets, bold colors, over-the-top acting, the extreme effects, everything. It’s so in your face that you can’t ignore it. I think it was different from other movies with similar themes in that it took the route of visually, viscerally showing how body dysmorphia and women’s fear of losing value as they age manifests into becoming someone they don’t recognize, and how you will sabotage and destroy your future self in the process of trying to fit into an unachievable ideal. The film asks - is it worth it? Nothing was played safe or sugarcoated. The messaging is simple but the execution was so effective.

Thank you for sharing your story and being so frank. I believe that one takeaway from this film is that it is pointless to worry too much about how others are going to perceive us. The constant vicious inner conflicts are not only detrimental to our mental health but also invariably end up affecting our social lives.  


I hope you find the support you need to feel confident in being the person you want to be, and that you do not allow others, or even yourself, to rob you of that confidence.

I wanted to like the movie so much, but I felt as though a ‘death by 1000 cuts’-type of thing happened during my viewing. There were so many little moments that took me out of the film that by end when blood is being sprayed everywhere I’m just sitting here completely checked out and thinking about what I wanna eat for dinner.

 All of these little moments are not nearly enough to ruin the overall movie, but they stacked up for me in such a way that it created this weird undercurrent of disinterest in its own premise that I lost interest too and made me actively dislike what I was seeing. Stuff like the whole process of transferring blood/The Substance (gravity and IV’s do not work that way), generic ‘evil company’ vibes that I feel like I’ve seen so many times before, getting a flashback for the French cookbook even though we saw her get it as a gift like 15 minutes ago, not even bothering to give proper names to the shows and talk shows. 

Maybe movies of this type aren’t really for me but even when things ramp up it felt like were a 14 year old’s vision of what would make people uncomfortable. That blood spraying scene at the end was more frustrating than funny. The cooking sequence came off as ‘lemme just fist a jar of mayo for a few minutes and layer that audio onto this cooking scene’.

I think the best part of the movie, and I saw it mentioned in another comment too, was when Demi Moore’s character tried to get ready for a date but kept getting sucked into her own insecurities until she didn’t even bother going. I thought that was an amazing scene, and maybe the whole movie didn’t need to be all that for me to like it but I definitely would’ve enjoyed more of it

I walked out of the theatre, and I have been looking for someone who saw what I saw, like a thirsty man in the desert since. Thank you, for that drink of water. 

I got so immensely bored of all the useless repetition, empty shots, and that every message is literally super signaled and pre-chewed for the audience, as if we're all imbeciles. 
There was just not enough material to fill the time and what was there was really pushed on you "see, see, see…?" 

The body horror aspects were so tame and self-conscious, I briefly wondered if I was seeing the same "crazy" movie? 

I really think people who enjoyed it are young and haven't seen many movies or I am missing something massive here.

It could just be a fun, yet deeply empty film to waste some time with, and I think if it was advertised like that I'd have enjoyed it more, but I definitely also would have waited for streaming. 
Just some jocky romp with zero Substance indeed.

I was amused it won a screenplay award. The concept is strong, the effects are good and nasty, but every line of dialogue is just what it seems to be (and usually gets repeated), no wit or irony or surprises at all. Can't even be arsed to give Sue a last name.

You're right, if it were just billed as a daring grossout it'd sit better with me. But it's being hailed as a clever satire, and from a North American POV, the showbiz details are all too far off the mark to feel like our real society is implicated: Sparkle won an Oscar at some point?
